learningObjectives.title: States of matter & changes of state

questions.q: Which equation correctly defines density?
options: density = mass × volume
density = mass ÷ volume
density = volume ÷ mass
density = mass ÷ weight
questions.explain: Density ρ = m/V: mass divided by volume. Its standard unit is kg/m³.

questions.q: A block of metal has a mass of 600 g and a volume of 75 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
A copper sample has a density of 8900 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.002 m³. Calculate its mass.
questions.explain: Rearranging ρ = m/V gives m = ρV = 8900 × 0.002 = 17.8 kg.

questions.q: Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³. What is the mass of 0.5 m³ of water?
An object of mass 240 kg has a density of 600 kg/m³. Calculate its volume.
questions.explain: Rearranging ρ = m/V gives V = m/ρ = 240 ÷ 600 = 0.4 m³.

questions.q: A solid object floats on water. What can you conclude about its density?
options: It is greater than the density of water
It is equal to the density of water
It is less than the density of water
It has no density because it floats
questions.explain: An object floats when its mean density is less than that of the fluid (water, 1000 kg/m³); denser objects sink.

questions.q: In which state of matter are the particles regularly arranged, touching, and only vibrating about fixed positions?
options: Gas
Liquid
Solid
Plasma
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are in a fixed, regular arrangement, held closely together, vibrating about fixed positions, which is why solids keep their shape.

questions.q: Why does a gas have a much lower density than the same substance as a solid?
options: The particles become lighter as a gas
The particles are much further apart in a gas, so the same mass fills a larger volume
Gas particles have more mass each
Mass is destroyed when a solid becomes a gas
questions.explain: Changing state does not change the number or mass of particles, but in a gas they are spread far apart, so the same mass occupies a far larger volume, giving a much lower density.

questions.q: When ice melts to form water, what happens to the total mass?
options: It increases
It decreases
It stays the same
It becomes zero
questions.explain: Melting is a physical change: no particles are created or destroyed, so mass is conserved. The water has the same mass as the ice it came from.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state when a liquid turns directly into a solid?
options: Condensing
Freezing
Evaporating
Sublimation
questions.explain: Liquid to solid is freezing (solidification). Gas to liquid is condensing; liquid to gas is evaporating/boiling.

questions.q: Why is a change of state described as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
options: A new substance is always made
The substance recovers its original properties if the change is reversed
Energy is destroyed during the change
The number of particles changes
questions.explain: Changes of state are physical: no new substance forms, and the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed (e.g. water refreezing to ice).

questions.q: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
options: Only the kinetic energy of the particles
Only the potential energy stored between particles
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles
The energy supplied by an external heater
questions.explain: Internal energy is the total energy stored by the particles: the sum of their kinetic energy (from motion) and the potential energy stored in the bonds/forces between them.

questions.q: Heating a substance without changing its state increases its internal energy. Specifically, it increases the particles'...
options: potential energy only, so temperature stays constant
kinetic energy, so the temperature rises
mass
number
questions.explain: When heating raises temperature (no state change), the energy increases the particles' kinetic energy, so they move faster and the temperature rises.

questions.q: A 2 kg block of aluminium (specific heat capacity 900 J/kg°C) is heated from 20°C to 70°C. Calculate the energy transferred.
How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0.5 kg of water (specific heat capacity 4200 J/kg°C) by 30°C?
On a heating graph, the temperature stays constant while a substance boils. What is happening to the energy supplied during this flat section?
options: It is being used to increase the particles' kinetic energy
It is being used to break the bonds between particles (increasing potential energy)
It is being lost and has no effect
It is reducing the mass of the substance
questions.explain: During a change of state the temperature is constant because the energy supplied breaks the bonds/forces between particles (raising potential energy), not their kinetic energy.

questions.q: What is the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance?
options: The energy to raise 1 kg by 1°C
The energy to change the state of 1 kg from liquid to gas with no temperature change
The energy to change the state of 1 kg from solid to liquid
The energy to melt 1 g of the substance
questions.explain: Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas (or back) at constant temperature. Latent heat of fusion refers to the solid↔liquid change.

questions.q: Calculate the energy needed to melt 2 kg of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 334 000 J/kg.
The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2 260 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to boil away 0.5 kg of water already at 100°C?
1 670 000 J of energy melts a block of ice (specific latent heat of fusion = 334 000 J/kg). What mass of ice was melted?
questions.explain: Rearranging E = mL gives m = E/L = 1 670 000 ÷ 334 000 = 5 kg.

questions.q: What causes the pressure of a gas on the walls of its container?
options: The weight of the gas particles resting on the walls
Gas particles colliding with the walls and exerting a force
The particles sticking to the walls
The walls attracting the particles
questions.explain: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the container walls; each collision exerts a tiny force, and the total over the wall area gives the pressure.

questions.q: What happens to the average kinetic energy of gas particles as the temperature of the gas increases?
options: It decreases
It stays the same
It increases
It depends on the container size
questions.explain: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles: raising the temperature increases their average kinetic energy, so they move faster.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas is heated in a sealed, rigid container (constant volume). What happens to the gas pressure?
options: It decreases because particles slow down
It increases because particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
It stays the same because volume is fixed
It becomes zero
questions.explain: Heating increases the particles' speed, so they collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force. With volume fixed, this raises the pressure.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is halved. According to pV = constant, the new pressure is...
options: halved
doubled
unchanged
quartered
questions.explain: At constant temperature pV is constant, so if V is halved, p must double to keep the product the same (Boyle's law).
